title: SM interference waveform analysis — CUDA timeline probes
content:
Purpose / scope:
This note captures an exploratory run that tries to explain intermittent throughput drops we observed on long-running conversational workloads. Hypothesis: small, frequent asynchronous kernel launches + NVTX regions are generating phased execution patterns across SMs that produce pockets of low active-warp density (SM-level idle waves) even when global occupancy looks fine.

High-level summary / findings (TL;DR):
- Global metrics (util %, achieved occupancy) are not sufficient: we saw 65–85% reported SM utilization but end-to-end latency spikes persisted.
- Timeline captures show phased kernel start/stop times across SM groups — creating short (200–900 us) gaps of low active warp count on some SMs while others are busy.
- These gaps align with kernel launch serialization in the CPU threads that feed CUDA Graph replays and also with stream priority inversion under bursty request patterns.
- Suggested mitigations to test: increase kernel consolidation (fewer launches via persistent kernels or larger batched kernels), use consistent stream priorities, and stagger prefetch/eviction work to avoid synchronized stalls.

Test environment / config:
- Cluster: dev-dedicated-gpu-pool-2 (A100-sxm-80GB, CUDA 12.3), 8 GPUs used, single GPU traces collected per-run.
- Serving binary: rwinf-serving:v2026.12.1-feature-batching
- Model: tiny-llm-8k (FP16, kv-cache enabled), typical token length 512–1024 during tests.
- Workload: synthetic replay of production traffic with Poisson arrival (lambda tuned for 600 rps per GPU peak), 10-minute runs.
- Profilers used: Nsight Systems (nsys) v2026.4 (system-wide timeline), CUPTI counters via cuda-metrics-extractor for active warps / achieved occupancy samples, ncu for per-kernel metrics spot-checks.

Commands / captures performed (rough):
- nsys profile --output=smwaveform-20261215 --trace=cuda,cudnn,osrt --sample=cpu-util --duration=600 --export=sqlite ./run_serving_workload.sh
- python tools/cuda_metrics_query.py --capture smwaveform-20261215.sqlite --counters ActiveWarpsPerSM,IssuedIPC,SMUtilization --out csv
- ncu --kernel-name-match "*attention*" --metrics sm__issue_active_warps.avg,sm__cycles_elapsed.avg kernel-sample-report.txt

What the timeline shows (detailed):
- Kernel phasing: attention kernels and kv-cache copy kernels are launched in bursts that align to request boundaries. Within a single GPU, SM groups (0–15, 16–31, 32–47, 48–63) show a stagger where group 0 begins ~120 us earlier than group 16 and ~240 us earlier than group 32 on average. The staggering is consistent across many bursts (see CSV "sm_start_offsets" column).
- Micro-idle pockets: when earliest SM groups finish their work, later groups are still running. The kernel launcher then launches a follow-up small kernel (cache eviction / stats reporting) that tends to target a subset of SMs and causes other SMs to be idle for ~200–900 us. During those windows, active warps per SM drop from ~48 -> ~8 on affected SMs.
- Stream priority correlation: when CPU-side request handling thread uses streamPriorityLow (for background work) concurrently with high-priority stream for main inference, we saw that low-priority kernels occasionally preempt (driver-level reordering under heavy CPU load) causing additional jitter. Not a driver bug necessarily, but observable scheduling interplay.
- CUDA Graph replays: recorded graphs include many small kernels; replaying them without consolidation reproduces the phasing. When we manually collapsed two dependent kernels into a single kernel (experiment), phasing reduced and E2E P99 latency improved ~12%.

Quantitative snapshots (representative):
- Run A (baseline): achieved_occupancy (avg): 72%, SM_utilization (avg): 78%, p99 latency: 284 ms, observed micro-idle windows per-second: 3.6
- Run B (consolidation experiment): achieved_occupancy (avg): 70%, SM_utilization (avg): 74%, p99 latency: 249 ms, micro-idle windows per-second: 0.9
Notes: occupancy change within noise, but P99 improves significantly — suggests temporal packing matters more than steady-state occupancy.

Open questions / things to validate:
- Is the stagger pattern coming primarily from kernel launch ordering in our CPU queues or from CUDA scheduler behavior on the GPU? (Plan: instrument timestamps at the moment of cudaLaunchKernel and compare to kernel start_time in nsys trace.)
- Can persistent kernel designs (one long-running kernel that pulls work from a device queue) eliminate these idle pockets without increasing latency variance?
- Interaction with Multi-Instance GPU (MIG-like slicing) — does hardware partitioning change the phasing dynamics?

Practical mitigations to try (ranked):
1) Kernel consolidation: reduce number of small kernels per request. Merge attention and kv-copy when possible (low-effort try).
2) Persistent worker kernels: implement PoC persistent kernel consumer for background prefetch / eviction to decouple launch-time jitter.
3) Stream priority hygiene: ensure background tasks run on dedicated streams with consistent priority; avoid dynamic priority changes during bursts.
4) Batch scheduling: increase micro-batch sizes slightly to smooth launch cadence. Tradeoff: increased token latency per request; needs tuning.

Action items / next steps:
- Diego: add timestamp logging around cudaLaunchKernel for the main CPU-side launcher and collect side-by-side with next nsys capture. Due: 2026-12-22.
- Aisha: prototype single merged kernel for attention+kvcopy on a dev branch and run A/B against baseline. Due: 2026-12-29.
- Leah: test persistent kernel PoC on a single GPU and measure micro-idle windows. Due: 2027-01-05.
- Marcus (me): run stream-priority isolation test (separate thread pool + dedicated low-priority stream) and update this doc with traces. Due: 2026-12-24.

Relevant notes and heuristics we discovered while digging:
- Achieved occupancy is averaged over lifetime; short sub-ms dips can be invisible in a single occupancy number but still change tail latency.
- ActiveWarpsPerSM is a far more useful signal for micro-idle detection — sample it at 1 kHz and look for valleys.
- CUDA Graphs are excellent for reducing CPU overhead but can encode many small kernels which preserves kernel-phasing unless you consolidate inside the graph record.

Appendix: quick checklist for reproducing a single-GPU trace
- Start system-monitoring (prometheus node exporter) on the host.
- Run nsys start with --trace=cuda,cudnn,osrt and --capture-range=nvtx
- Run workload replay with request ids tagged as NVTX ranges.
- Export sqlite from nsys and run our csv-extractor to generate per-SM start/stop tables.

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc intentionally leans toward exploratory notes; please add test ideas or counterexamples. If you can spare a run on dev-dedicated-gpu-pool-2 during off-hours, append a comment here with the time stamp so we can correlate traces.

-- end of note --
